messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet Truong, a 44-year-old nurse of South Eastern Asian descent, still recalls the night he was mugged on his way home from a late shift at the hospital. It was a chilly autumn evening, and the dimly lit alleyway behind the building seemed like a shortcut to save time. As he walked, lost in thought about an upcoming patient's surgery, two men emerged from the shadows, their faces obscured by hoods. The next few minutes were a blur of chaos – Kiet remembers trying to shield his face as one attacker punched him while the other rummaged through his pockets. The pain in his jaw and temple still lingers in vivid detail, as if his body is replaying the assault with every flashback. The days that followed were marked by an increasing sense of hypervigilance. Kiet found himself constantly scanning the environment for potential threats – a habit he justified to himself as a necessary precaution in his line of work. On the job, he would meticulously check patients' rooms and corridors for any signs of danger, much to the confusion of his colleagues. At home, he would position himself near exits and scrutinize every stranger who walked by his house, convinced that the muggers might return. His wife, Linh, began to notice a change in him – how he'd jump at every creak of the floorboard or insist on sitting with his back against the wall at restaurants. As Kiet's anxiety intensified, so did his reliance on mental distractions. He would keep his mind occupied by mentally rehearsing patient care scenarios, analyzing medical charts, or replaying conversations from the day – anything to stave off the haunting memories of that night. Even in quiet moments, like during meditation or reading before bed, Kiet's thoughts would drift back to the mugging, and he'd relive the physical pain and fear all over again. Sleep became a luxury Kiet could no longer afford. He would lie awake for hours, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios – of being attacked again, of failing to protect himself or others. When he did manage to drift off, it was only to be jolted awake by the sound of footsteps outside or the rustling of leaves. His body seemed to have internalized the trauma, responding to every minor stimulus as if it were a life-or-death threat. One day, while on his rounds at the hospital, Kiet caught himself frantically searching for an escape route from a patient's room – a stark realization that his hypervigilance had started to compromise his work. That was when he knew he needed help. The weight of his memories, coupled with the crushing sense that nothing good could ever happen to him again, had become too much to bear. Kiet feared that if he couldn't shake off this all-consuming anxiety, it would ultimately destroy not just his career but also his relationships and his very sense of self. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with the sleeve of his jacket – a habitual gesture he'd developed since the mugging – Kiet revealed the despair that had taken hold: "I feel like I'm stuck in this nightmare, reliving it over and over, with no way out." His eyes pleaded for reassurance that there was still hope, that somehow, someway, he could rediscover a future worth living.
